messages.content: Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.
Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.

samples.text: Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, the rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude of the intermediate sum, causing a different rounding error than if you first add the other two numbers. Consequently, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce different floating‑point results, breaking associativity.

Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, the rounding can occur after the first two operands (a + b) and then again after adding the third, or it can occur after adding b + c first, producing different rounded intermediates. Because these intermediate rounding errors can differ, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) may yield distinct floating‑point results, breaking associativity.

Consequently, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce different floating‑point results, showing that addition is not associative in this representation.

In floating‑point arithmetic each number is stored with a finite number of bits, so every operation is rounded to the nearest representable value. When three numbers are added, the rounding can occur after the first addition, changing the intermediate result that is then used in the second addition. As a result, \((a+b)+c\) and \(a+(b+c)\) can yield different rounded results, so floating‑point addition is not associative.
